newsitem.title: USA: WMX Buntrock plans exit upon CEO's arrival.
newsitem.headline: WMX Buntrock plans exit upon CEO's arrival.

text.p: WMX Technologies Inc focused renewed attention Friday on its search for a chief executive by saying that chairman and acting chief executive Dean Buntrock plans to step aside when a new skipper comes aboard.
"Dean has indicated that he has no plans to participate in the management of the company once a new CEO is elected," said WMX spokesman Bill Plunkett.
"He'd like to remain on the board, clearly. He wants to be in a position to provide counsel and support to the new CEO," Plunkett said.

The company's comment on Buntrock's plans followed a mid-February suggestion by Nell Minow, a principal at the Lens Inc investment group, that Buntrock should find a new CEO, then exit. Any top-quality leader stepping into WMX would demand as much, Minow said.
Lens owns a stake in Oak Brook, Ill.-based WMX, the largest U.S. garbage hauling concern. Other major investors in recent weeks have reportedly echoed Minow's concerns.
Plunkett said: "Dean is just trying to clarify his position ... He feels it's important that the company attract the best chief executive it can and he wants to do that."
Analysts said the Buntrock statement may mean WMX is close to hiring a new chief, but also said it likely will only aggravate uncertainties running through the WMX rank and file.
"WMX needs one person at the top to sort of orchestrate a consistent message and they really don't have that now," said Argus research analyst James Kelleher.
"Every aspect of their operations has this sort of Peyton Place tinge to it now," he said.
Wall Street is looking toward WMX's expected Monday announcement of quarterly financial results with a yawn.
The company is expected to report earnings of $0.38 per share, flat against the same period a year ago, according to the First Call consensus of 10 analysts' forecasts.
"For them to beat that substantially would be a huge surprise ... Even if they're slightly above it, though, I wouldn't expect any movement on the stock," said Parker/Hunter analyst Richard Sporrer.
"The stock is moving now on this restructuring, selling assets, finding a new CEO, that sort of thing," Sporrer said.

After months of demands for better performance from major investors, WMX on February 4 unveiled a sweeping restructuring plan. Two weeks later, WMX chief executive Phillip Rooney unexpectedly resigned and long-time chairman Buntrock stepped in on a temporary basis to handle the CEO responsibilities.
